old: For one who practises it accomplishes two aims at once: health and mastery of the senses. That good conduct (sadvṛtta) we shall teach in full, O Agniveśa. It is as follows. One should honour gods, cows, brahmins, teachers, elders, adepts (siddha) and preceptors; tend the fire; wear approved herbs; perform ablution (upasparśa) at the two times; frequently keep the excretory passages and the feet clean; have the hair, beard, body-hair and nails cut three times a fortnight; always wear unsoiled clothes, and be cheerful (sumanas) and fragrant; be well-dressed, with well-kept hair, regularly oiling the head, ears, nose and feet, taking medicated smoke (dhūma), the first to speak, pleasant-faced, a helper in difficulties, one who offers oblations, who sacrifices, who gives, who pays homage to crossroads, who presents offerings (bali), who honours guests, who gives rice-balls (piṇḍa) to the ancestors, who at the right time speaks what is beneficial, measured, sweet and meaningful, self-controlled, righteous (dharmātman), emulous in the means but not envious of the result, free from worry, fearless, modest, intelligent, highly energetic, skilful, forbearing, righteous (dhārmika), a believer (āstika), and one who serves those senior in discipline, intellect, learning, lineage and age, the adepts and the preceptors; one should walk about with an umbrella, a staff, a headdress and footwear, looking a yoke's length ahead; be given to auspicious practices; avoid dirty rags, bones, thorns, impure things, hair, husks, rubbish heaps, ashes, potsherds, and bathing and offering grounds; stop exercise before fatigue; be a kinsman to all living beings; be a pacifier of the angry, a comforter of the frightened, a helper of the distressed, true to one's word, given chiefly to conciliation (sāman), tolerant of others' harsh words, a destroyer of intolerance, one who sees the merit of tranquillity, and a destroyer of the causes of attachment and aversion.

old: Prose, not a verse. old: One should not take food without a gem in the hand, unbathed, in soiled clothes, without japa (recitation), without offering oblations to the deities, without making an offering to the ancestors, without giving to teachers, guests and dependants, without a pleasant fragrance, without a garland, with hands, feet and face unwashed, with an unclean mouth, facing north, distracted, with attendants who are not devoted, ill-mannered, impure or hungry, in impure vessels, in an improper place, at an improper time, in a crowded place, without giving the first portion to the fire, unsprinkled with sprinkling-water, unconsecrated with mantras, while reviling it, food that is reviled, or food served by an unfriendly person. One should not take stale food, except meat, greens (haritaka), dried vegetables, fruits and baked foods (bhakṣya); one should not eat leaving no remainder, except curd, honey, salt, roasted barley-flour (saktu) and ghee (sarpis); one should not eat curd at night; one should not eat saktu alone, nor at night, nor after a meal, nor in large amount, nor twice, nor with water in between, nor bite it with the teeth (dvija) before eating.
